title: Counting, extended binomial and partial fractions
summary: Count arrangements and selections with permutations and combinations, expand (1 + x)ⁿ for fractional and negative n, and split rational expressions into partial fractions.

keyterms.definition: If one choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, together they can be made in m × n ways.
An arrangement of objects where order matters; ⁿPᵣ = n! / (n − r)!.
A selection of objects where order does not matter; ⁿCᵣ = n! / (r!(n − r)!).
n objects with groups of identical items can be arranged in n! / (p! q! …) ways.
(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)x²/2! + … for any rational n; infinite unless n ∈ ℕ.
The values of x for which an infinite binomial series converges: |x| < 1 for (1 + x)ⁿ.
Writing a rational expression as a sum of simpler fractions with linear denominators, e.g. A/(x − a) + B/(x − b).
A rational expression whose numerator has lower degree than its denominator.

questions.prompt: In how many ways can the letters of MATHS be arranged?
questions.explanation: Five different letters: 5! = 120.

questions.prompt: How many committees of 3 can be chosen from 8 people?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter: ⁸C₃ = 56. 336 = ⁸P₃ counts ordered selections.
⁶P₂ = 6 × 5 = 30: six choices for first place, then five for second.
Combinations are selections; permutations are arrangements where order matters.

questions.prompt: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of LEVEL are there?
questions.explanation: Five letters with two Ls and two Es: 5! / (2! × 2!) = 30.

questions.prompt: Five people sit in a row. In how many arrangements are two particular people next to each other?
questions.explanation: Treat the pair as one block: 4! arrangements, times 2 for the order inside the block = 48.

questions.text: A 4-digit PIN using digits 0–9 with repetition allowed has ___ possibilities.
questions.explanation: Product principle: 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10⁴. 5040 would forbid repeated digits.
Each selection of r objects can be ordered in r! ways.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to its count.

pairs.left: Arrange 6 different books on a shelf
Award gold and silver among 6 runners
Set each of 6 switches on or off

questions.explanation: Ask: are we arranging or selecting, and is repetition allowed?

lessons.title: Extended binomial theorem and partial fractions

questions.explanation: With n = −1 the coefficients are 1, −1, (−1)(−2)/2! = 1, …, so signs alternate.

questions.prompt: For which x is the expansion of (1 − 2x)^½ valid?
questions.explanation: The series in (1 + u)ⁿ needs |u| < 1; here u = −2x, so |2x| < 1.

questions.text: For small x, (1 + x)^½ ≈ 1 + ½x ___ (up to the x² term).
questions.explanation: The x² coefficient is (½)(−½)/2! = −⅛.

questions.statement: The expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ for a negative or fractional n is an infinite series.
questions.explanation: The coefficients never reach zero, so the series does not terminate.

questions.prompt: For which x is the binomial expansion of (2 + x)⁻¹ valid?
questions.explanation: Write (2 + x)⁻¹ = ½(1 + x/2)⁻¹, which needs |x/2| < 1.
5 = A(x + 4) + B(x − 1). x = 1 gives A = 1; x = −4 gives B = −1.

questions.statement: Before splitting into partial fractions, the degree of the numerator should be less than the degree of the denominator.
questions.explanation: If not, divide first so you have a polynomial plus a proper rational expression.

questions.prompt: Match each binomial power to a fact about its expansion.

pairs.right: Finite expansion, valid for all x

questions.explanation: Only natural-number powers give finite expansions valid for every x.

items: Check that the fraction is proper
